title: Kumbhakarna Tells the Truth
hookLine: drums, conches and elephants wake a giant; he tells his brother the king the truth, and then has to choose
carry: dharma is knowing the right, then choosing it
tomorrow: why does a temple sing God awake each morning?

cards: Drums are pounding. Conches are blowing. People are shouting into a giant's ears, and elephants are being led over his sleeping body.
Next to him, food is heaped up for the moment his eyes open. It's Lanka, in Valmiki's Ramayana, and the city is under siege. Ravana needs his brother Kumbhakarna, and Kumbhakarna is asleep.
Getting him up takes a crowd. Today, what a giant says when he finally wakes, and what he does next.

teach.b: We met Kumbhakarna's sleep earlier this week: the boon that went wrong, tamas, the pull to stay under. Today is about him awake.
He eats, he's brought to his brother, and Ravana tells him everything: the taking of Sita, the army at the walls. And the sleepy giant tells the king the truth to his face.

Paraphrased: you did this without listening to counsel; you did first what should have come after. He isn't the first to say it. Their younger brother Vibhishana had already told Ravana: give Sita back.
Ravana insulted him, and Vibhishana left and crossed over to Rama.
So the Ramayana sets three brothers side by side. Ravana knows, and won't listen. Vibhishana knows, and acts, and it costs him his home.
Kumbhakarna knows, says it plainly, and then goes out to fight for his brother anyway, and falls to Rama. Here is the teaching, named plainly: dharma, what's right, isn't only something you know.
It's something you choose. Kumbhakarna's honesty is real, and many retellings honor his loyalty. But the tradition still remembers which side he chose.
On Dussehra, in many towns in North India, Ravana's giant effigy burns, and beside it, Kumbhakarna's and Meghanada's. And Vibhishana, the one who walked out, is the one Rama makes king of Lanka.
The today step is hard and familiar: knowing someone you love is wrong, and standing with them anyway. The Ramayana doesn't say love your family less.
It says loyalty doesn't make the wrong thing right. And one careful note: tiredness that won't lift is a matter for a doctor, never a mark of bad character.

how: Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana are retold in Ramayana tellings and Ramlila performances, and on Dussehra many towns in North India burn effigies of Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Meghanada.

o: a rule kept only by kings and sages
loyalty to family, which makes any side right
dharma: the right thing known, and then chosen

games.q: three brothers, one choice — tap the pairs.
p: tells Ravana the truth, then fights for him
tells the truth and crosses to Rama

s: once awake, Kumbhakarna praises Ravana's plan
he tells him plainly that he acted without listening to counsel.
Rama makes Vibhishana king of Lanka
the brother who acted on what was right is the one Lanka is given to.
in the Ramayana, loyalty to family makes the wrong side right
Kumbhakarna's honesty and loyalty are honored, and he still fell fighting for the wrong.

games.q: you're Vibhishana. you told Ravana to give Sita back, and he insulted you in front of the court. what do you do?
o: stay quiet and fight for him.
leave, and cross over to Rama.
go to sleep, like your brother.
games.why: Vibhishana leaves and goes to Rama, who welcomes him and makes him king of Lanka. dharma known, then chosen: the step Kumbhakarna didn't take.

practice: Let one place come to mind where you know what's right and haven't chosen it yet, maybe with someone you love. Let it sit in front of you while you breathe, without scolding yourself.

Then find the smallest step that would choose it, one sentence or one look, and hold it lightly. If you pray, say Rama's name softly, Shri Ram, and ask for Vibhishana's courage; if you don't, just hold the step.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. Kumbhakarna's long sleep, and his waking: the truth told plainly, and the choice he made after. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dharma: what's right, the order that holds life together, and one's duty within it.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is knowing the right, then choosing it. The giant knew. Go gently.
